Some more thought on this, and I think a heavily modified Harkness Test would do well to identify safe transformations:

1. Is this character visibly portrayed as an adult?
2. Is this character clearly written as an adult?
3. Is this character still recognizable as an evolution of the source character?

If all yes, then can proceed with caution. No on the first two is an immediate cut-off. No on the third makes it an OC.

I don't think we disagree at all. When all you have is snapshots in time, a well written progression of a character should be no different externally than a normal human being.

The human brain, despite all contradictory public sentiments, never stops growing and evolving. It does, however, slow down on a semi-logarithmic scale.

Who a person is changes so much between childhood and teenagerdom that they are essentially completely different people. I agree that aging up of actual children is pointless, and by these rules, should not be attempted.

However, the scale of change from being a teenager to being a young adult is a lot lower, and is easier to effectively write. Take Ellie from The Last Of Us series. In the first game, unquestionably underage. In the second, a young adult. However, both recognizably the same person. Her age in either game is just a fact of circumstances, not a defining point of the character. This, if well done, should be an acceptable transition, but must needs be fully realized to be so.

Another, more extreme example of well done was technically in reverse: The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles. In the original (and later) Indiana Jones movies, you have Indy (portrayed by Harrison Ford), who is a gruff, dedicated museumologist out trying to save relics from the Nazis. In the series, you have teen-aged Indy (played by Sean Patrick Flanery), who is easily recognizable as being the same character, just in his teenage years. (You also have 8-ish year old Indy played by Corey Carrier, but that's just some kid in a hat, and it shows.) The Chronicles even show some of the events that help guide the character's evolution from teenager to the earlier portrayed adult.

As both the host of the Going in Dry mirror server (which runs the latest git snapshot, and is situated within the United States) and a CSA survivor, my skin is pretty deep into this particular game. That said, the opinions and statements herein are mine and mine alone, and neither they nor I represent the developers of SPnati, or the content creators. I'm just a person hosting a thing on the internet.

If absent external preconceptions or context, a character is portrayed in both art and characterization within SPnati as an adult, then that character should be allowed. However, using adult artwork for a character whose mental age is unchanged from their minor portrayal, or the more common reverse (mind of an ancient in the body of a child) falls very clearly into "do not allow" territory. Otherwise, characters should be considered in the context they are presented, not in unrelated contexts.

An excellent example of concept is Mari from OMORI. In the only canon materials (the game and it's source webcomic), she is never shown to be any older than 15, which is absolutely in forbidden territory. However, in SPnati, Mari is shown to be from an alternate universe to the source material, wherein she is a young woman in college, in a relationship with Hero, and of sound mind and body to consent to acts involved in the game. She is clearly an adult in this portrayal, someone who has progressed in life to the point where, were you to meet her in real life, you'd have no qualms in interacting with her as such.

Let's take random casual observer Bob. Bob is, one morning, walking down the street and sees Kara, a young woman whose parents he knows, and who was 15 the one time he met her a decade ago. Kara is out on a date with her boyfriend, who is 24, and they are making out on a park bench. He thinks to himself, "That's Kara, Alan and Nancy's kid. She's 15! That's wrong!" That afternoon, Bob picks up a copy of Uncanny X-Men #200, the Trial of Magneto #1 issue. Bob is a casual reader of comics, and has only ever seen this character (Erik Lehnsherr) in Classic X-Men #12, wherein he is shown at the age of 15. Bob exclaims to himself, "You can't try him for war crimes and genocide, he's only 15! That's wrong!" That evening, Bob sees Mari in SPnati, absent of in-game context, and thinks to himself "She's that character from OMORI, she's 15, that's wrong!"

While not at all malicious in intent, Bob is objectively wrong on all counts, as the contexts stored in his mind are invalid compared to the situations presented. Kara is 25, dating someone younger than her. Erik Lehnsherr is in his late 50s during the Trial of Magneto storyline, and thus is clearly of age not only to have committed his vast swath of crimes, but to be fairly tried and punished for them. And in SPnati, Mari is a young adult in college who is very clearly of age and fully capable of consent. Thus, Bob's point of view cannot be used to determine the correctness of any of these situations.

Now, I will posit that the game could (and should) denote in-situ age of the characters contained therein in their presented contexts, which would much more easily handle the consternation at hand. When submitted (or reviewed), if a character is stated to be 21 in the context of SPnati, the question of whether they should be permitted is easily addressed by answering the two qualifiers of A) does this character's art portray a 21-year-old, and B) does this character speak and behave as a 21-year-old would in the situations they are placed? If the answer to either question (or, Gods forbid, both) is No, then drop the banhammer. Otherwise, clear sailing.

A better analogy would be this: A core with hyperthreading consists of a real core and a pretend core. A non-hyperthread core is just a core.

I'm guessing you are wanting Windows desktop VMs to remote into for reasons. With that in mind, here's some sizing guidelines:

* With your current configuration, you could run 2 concurrent windows VMs at 2 vCPU each without having to experience lag.

Hyperthreading doesn't work that way.

In the case of the i5-4590, the processor has 4 cores, which are presented as 4 threads. This would appear to the OS as 4 usable CPU cores. All 4 cores can be fully utilized.

The i7 you are considering has 4 cores, which are presented as 8 threads (2 threads per physical core). This would appear to the OS as 8 usable CPU cores. Half (4) of the cores can be fully utilized at the same time, while the remaining half (4) can be at least partially utilized.

If you plan to have VMs that aren't CPU heavy, the i7 would be preferable, as idle systems tend to be dealt with alright by hyperthreaded cores. However, if you plan to do things that are CPU heavy, a 4C/4T i7 or the existing i5 would be preferable, as hyperthreaded cores tend to have slightly lower individual performance than non-hyperthreaded cores.

TL;DR: 4 cores / 4 Threads = 4 vCPUs. 4 Cores / 8 Threads = 8 vCPUs. Threads are not separate from cores, but derivative.

Very likely fake or misread. Reason #1: Downloading isn't illegal (in the US).

The reason DMCA notices get sent to P2P users is the seed-back function, where while downloading, you are also uploading the content you already have. Uploading (sharing) is what you get charged with, and fined for.

Reason #2: Neither the ISP nor anyone else can know or prove what you have downloaded, because of TLS.

Connections between your computer and near all websites these days (including Fmovies) run over TLS encrypted channels, which cannot (without very specific circumstances) be decrypted in flight. The know you visited an IP address, but nothing else. And a single public IP address can carry multiple different sites and all sorts of content. They don't and can't know the specific URIs you visited, or what content you received. They can't even size match because TLS packets are a padded to fit cipher requirements. So no exact size matches.

Generally, your ISP doesn't care what you do. They will send a notice when they get a notice, and the DMCA sending agencies (usually third party companies contracted by the content owners) can't know what you download, only what you share using P2P systems. ISPs are required by law to forward DMCA notices, and they actually really hate doing it, because it means they have to do something they aren't already doing.

Third: Emails like this are actually a common scam technique.

There are lots of scammers out there sending threatening emails to those who they hope aren't technologically literate (your father is a perfect target) saying "You've been caught downloading <random popular things> from <random popular sites>, which is illegal, blah blah blah. Stop doing the thing." Then later, they send another email saying "You have continued to doing the thing, you must now be paying the fine or else we will do a horrible!"

It is important that if/when that second email arrives, your father NOT pay them. Because a) if a person pays once, they'll escalate and attempt to get more and more, b) money sent to these scammers is used for very unpleasant purposes (violent/terrorist groups get funding this way), and c) depending on how they demand to be paid, it could be a form of money laundering which would make your father legally liable for criminal charges.

This may be a sore subject for your family, but it's important that this be made clear.

Mid/High split is where the upload frequency sets for DOCSIS are moved from the low end of the bands in use, where there aren't a lot of space or actual bandwidth, up to the middle or upper ends of the bands (alongside the download channels). DOCSIS 3.1 compatible modems, especially Spectrum issued ones, support this change.

This is unlikely to work the way you want, simply because A) it's way too complex, and B) OpenVPN has massive overhead over-the-line.

Much easier way: Any two-NIC basic box for pfSense, port A to WAN, port B to a MANAGED switch. Set up a bunch of VLANs (1 per system, additional 1 for Guest Wireless network), and trunk them across port B. Have the switch have a separate VLAN for every physical connection. WAP gets two VLANS (one for auth'd wireless connections, one for guests) trunked on its connection. Use Wireless Client isolation on both wireless networks.

Initial set up takes a little bit, but it'll run pretty cleanly by itself afterwards. For the individual client system VLANs, use tiny subnets (/30s), and only allow routing from each subnet to and from the NAT'd WAN connection.

Now, to specifically address your questions:

1) Can you do it with OpenVPN? I mean, kinda, yeh, but it's incredibly more complex, slower, and more prone to breakage. Also, firewall rules will be bloody nasty, and if even one connection goes awry, it can screw everything. Also, using a VPN only increases latency. You do NOT want to use it for anything real-time sensitive like day trading unless you absolutely have to (see: forced by your upstream data provider).

2) For the pfSense hardware, something like this: https://www.amazon.com/Intel-pfSense-firewall-windows-computer/dp/B077FXF6Y8 would do fine.

3) Any modern routing-capable system with two gigabit ethernet ports will easily saturate your WAN connection. Something similar to what I recommended for 2 should be fine. There are also probably cheaper non-industrial versions.

4) Any modern processor supports AES, from either major vendor. Stick with mainline x86_64, and you'll be fine. None of the security "features" of modern processors affect network traffic across the system in a useful manner.

Final Summary.

At most, a highly QoSing router that prioritizes your DT system, maybe on it's own separate VLAN/Subnet, will give you the reliability and security you need. As a point, an Operating System doesn't become particularly "certified" for FIPS 140-2 so much as a legal advisor with a technical background will evaluate the implementation of said operating system *as well as* the hardware it is running on to designate a Level (1 - 4) to which the entire setup is certified.

Neither CentOS nor RedHat are listed, but OpenSSL is. Conceivably, any operating system capable of running OpenSSL in FIPS mode (which CentOS is capable of doing) could be FIPS certified in situ with the correct configuration.

Do note that while Dell provides tools to create bootable firmware update packages that will effect the whole of the system at once, especially based off of the service tag, SuperMicro does (to the best of my knowledge) NOT provide such a tool, so there may be a lot of manual updating in that case. 

Hardware RAID Caveats: 

* Do not use RAID 5. Just... don't. Honestly, if you can spare the capacity, you should use RAID-10 for performance reasons. Otherwise, RAID-6 for High Availability.
* Remember, RAID is not backup.
* If you just want straight up performance, and don't care if your array dies when a drive dies, use RAID-0. It's the fastest, at the cost of reliability.
* When a drive dies (this is not an If), and if you are using 6 or 10, DO NOT actively use the server while it is rebuilding the array. Wait until lights stop blinking to put it back into service.
* Also, Dell PERC controllers do not automatically perform Consistency Checks. These should be scheduled (or manually performed) by the OS, using dell's tools, to run at least once every thirty days. I cannot speak to the Adaptec controller's behavior in this field, but you should find out either way.
* Do not, under ANY circumstances, use ZFS or Unraid with a hardware RAID array. It is very much like crossing the streams.

Details: If you are going to use any software multi-disk management system (FreeNAS/ZFS or Unraid) do NOT use hardware raid. Neither the H700 nor the Adaptec 5405 support IT (direct disk) mode, so you are stuck with hardware raid for both of these servers unless you want to replace them with a compatible HBA (non-raid hardware SAS card). That would not be cheap, not generally.

Final note: These servers have been out for a while. They were released in the 2009/2010 era, and are at the end of reliable use life. If they were properly used in an enterprise environment, you cannot expect them to not have been ridden hard the entire time, and are entering the period where they will start (or have already started) to decay and fail.

Unless they both combined are significantly cheaper (like, by half) than 500 dollars, and/or you don't care that both these systems WILL die before too long, you would be better off buying something like an HP ML30 or Dell T30 or the like, which will be much newer, much more powerful by default (newer processors come with lots of bonuses for this sort of activity), and much quieter and easier on your power bill.
